content.content:
The tool seems failing. Perhaps we can answer based on known knowledge. I know approximate years:

Hydrogen: Recognized as a distinct element by Henry Cavendish in 1766 (published 1766). Some credit to Cavendish for discovering hydrogen gas ("inflammable air") and then Antoine Lavoisier named it in 1783.

Helium: Discovered in the Sun's spectrum by Jules Janssen and Norman Lockyer in 1868, isolated on Earth by William Ramsay in 1895. But year of discovery as element: 1868 for spectral observation, 1895 for isolation. The question likely expects the discoverer of helium as the solar discovery (Janssen/Lockyer, 1868). Could note that.

Lithium: Discovered by Johan August Arfvedson in 1817 (in petalite mineral) while working with Jöns Jakob Berzelius.

Beryllium: Discovered by Louis Nicolas Vauquelin in 1798 (as a new element from beryl and emerald). However the isolation of pure beryllium metal was later by Friedrich Wöhler and Antoine Bussy in 1828. So discoverer credited Vauquelin, 1798.

Boron: Discovered by Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis Jacques Thenard in 1808 (they independently discovered). Also earlier by Humphry Davy in 1808? Actually Boron was first isolated by Sir Humphry Davy in 1808, but the element was discovered earlier by Gay-Lussac and Thenard (1808). The credit is shared.

Thus answer: Hydrogen - Henry Cavendish, 1766 (published); Helium - Jules Janssen (spectral) / Norman Lockyer, 1868; Lithium - Johan August Arfvedson, 1817; Beryllium - Louis Nicolas Vauquelin, 1798; Boron - Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis Jacques Thénard (and Humphry Davy), 1808.

content:
**First 5 elements of the periodic table – discoverers and year of discovery**

| Element (Atomic #) | Discoverer(s) | Year of discovery* | Notable details |
|--------------------|---------------|-------------------|-----------------|
| **Hydrogen (1)**   | Henry Cavendish (who called it “inflammable air”) | **1766** (published 1766) | Cavendish produced the gas by reacting metals with dilute acids and showed it was a distinct substance. Antoine Lavoisier later gave it the name “hydrogen” in 1783. |
| **Helium (2)**     | Jules Janssen (solar spectrum) & Norman Lockyer (independently identified the same line) | **1868** (solar observation) – isolated on Earth by William Ramsay in **1895** | The element was first detected as a bright yellow line in the Sun’s spectrum during a solar eclipse (Janssen, France) and simultaneously identified by Lockyer (UK). Ramsay later obtained the gas from cleveite. |
| **Lithium (3)**    | Johan August Arfvedson (working in J. J. Berzelius’s lab) | **1817** | While analysing the mineral petalite, Arfvedson recognized a new “alkaline earth” component that later became lithium. The metal itself was isolated later (by William Thomas Brande, 1821). |
| **Beryllium (4)**  | Louis Nicolas Vauquelin (from beryl & emerald) | **1798** | Vauquelin dissolved beryl in acid and precipitated a new oxide, which he named “beryllia.” Pure metallic beryllium was first produced by Friedrich Wöhler & Antoine Bussy in 1828. |
| **Boron (5)**      | Joseph Louis Gay‑Lussac & Louis Jacques Thénard (chemical synthesis) – also Sir Humphry Davy (electro‑reduction) | **1808** | Gay‑Lussac & Thénard obtained a substance they called “boracic acid” from borax. Davy, using electro‑lysis, isolated a brittle metal and confirmed it as a new element. The discovery is therefore credited jointly to the three chemists. |

\*The “year of discovery” refers to the first experimental identification of the element as a distinct substance. In cases where the element was first observed astronomically (helium) or first isolated later (beryllium, lithium, boron), the initial identification year is listed, with a note on subsequent isolation.
